articleTitle: Gems from the Science Museum: Five electrotechnological artifacts are selected as representative of the outstanding historical collection of London's Science Museum
abstract: 1838 The first electric telegraph, installed between Paddigton and West Drayton, a distance of 13 miles, by cooks and wheatstone, used five wires operated in pairs, thus parmitting 20 litters to be transmitted. Only this instrument and its companion, now in Berlin's postal museum, were produced.

articleTitle: Gems from the Deutsches Museum: Noteworthy historical artifacts from this Munich showplace are described
Air and sea rescue via satellite systems: Even experimental systems have helped survivors of air and sea accidents. Two different approaches are discussed
abstract: Passengers and crews members of sinking ships or crashed airplanes will stand a better chance of rescue anywhere in the world with a new system of emergency alert via satellite. The system will serve private and corporate fliers as well as airline crews; pleasure boaters and small-scale commercial fisherman as well as merchant shippers. Whether a plane has gone down in a remote mountain range or a ship is floundering in the subarctic Atlantic, satellites will detect distress signals and alert rescue teams.

articleTitle: The machine as partner of the new professional: Today's instruments are providing more data than the mind can process; expert systems are coming to the rescue but may soon usurp human roles
abstract: No one can truly predict the future, and many will refuse to believe that letters like the one above will ever be written, let alone in only 50 years. But during the relatively short history of electrotechnology, professional work has already undergone radical changes. Now the forces that produce change are increasing, and the pace of change is quickening. I believe it is safe to predict that advances in electrotechnology—and especially in automated decision making, or so-called knowledge systems—will dramatically alter the nature of professional work as we know it.

articleTitle: Digital audio is compact and rugged: High-density pitted disks in conjunction with sharply focused, precision-tracking laser pickup provide quality sound reproduction
abstract: From the blare of brass and the thunder of percussion to the whispering pianissimo of a solo violin, a whole range of sound is now captured and reproduced with new clarity and precision by what has come to be known as the compact-disk digital audio system. In that system a plastic disk only 12 centimeters in diameter digitally stores more than 1 hour of music in micrometer-size pits arranged in a spiral track on one side of the disk. A laser beam in the player reads the information optically off the rotating disk without touching its surface [Fig. 1].

articleTitle: In pursuit of the one-month chip: The objective is to describe the functions required of an as yet nonexistent integrated circuit, then have it delivered in 31 days or less
abstract: Dramatic progress electronic engineering seems to run roughly in 12-year cycles. The transistor was invented in 1947, the integrated circuit in 1959, and the microprocessor in 1971. The next big development? Many engineers are heralding the so-called one-month chip - the design, fabrication, and testing of an IC not in the usual months or years, but in 31 days.

"Money is the main reward—in fact, it is the only thing thai keeps me sane," said a 40-year-old development engineer wtio works for a very large computer company. He is unhappy with the progof his career and wants to go into management. "The first chance I get," he said, "I'll chuck my work station and go for the gold."

articleTitle: Communications: Long-distance fiber-optic networks, direct-broadcast satellites, and low-cost PBXs bring increased communications capacity to customers
abstract: Advances in communications technology over the past year are bringing greater communications capacity to individual users at economical cost. Especially notable are these developments: • The start of long-distance telephone and television service via optical fibers. • The beginning of direct-broadcast-satellite television services to the northeastern United States and the first widespread commercial use of the high-frequency Ku-band for satellite communications. • The availability of low-cost, high-performance satellite terminals, making satellite services accessible to small users. • The advent of low-cost private branch exchanges along with approval of the IEEE 802 local-area network standard, facilitating communication between computers and other devices.

articleTitle: Medical electronics: Biomedical engineers are exploiting electric signals to and from the body to aid rehabilitation of the handicapped
abstract: Twenty months ago 3 bullet intended for another man shattered the spine of Bassam Khawam, paralyzing him from the waist down, Doctors told Mr. Khawam, a 24-year old industrial engineer who lives in Cleveland, Ohio, that he would never walk again. But last April he showed an audience at the national convention of the Spinal Cord Society in St. Paul, Minn., that he could walk. By pressing a switch on his electronic walker, Mr. Khawam triggered a sequence of electric pulses from electrodes inserted into his leg muscles. These pulses, with their timing and voltage programmed by a computer strapped to Mr. Khawam's waist, caused first one leg and then the other to step forward.

articleTitle: International data wars are brewing: U.S. telecommunications deregulation, Third World protectionism, and European privacy regulations may complicate or curtail data flow across borders
abstract: The prospect of what one electronics executive calls an “information war” is threatening the international telecommunications grid on which modern business depends for moving data around the world. For most of its history, this grid has operated reasonably well, through the cooperation of national telecommunications agencies and companies. But in the last few years, three developments have started to disrupt this cooperation and may lead to growing confrontations and conflicts.

In the information society of the twenty-first century, as Japan sees it, communications will encompass telephone, television, data, and other systems. The system Japan is planning, called the Information Network System (INS), will be all digital, a blend of computer and telecommunications technologies. Using several transmission media-copper wire, optical-fiber cable, satellites, and radio - the system will tie telephones; data, facsimile, and video terminals; switching systems; and computers into one network, digitally carrying not only the human voice, but also data and still and moving picture.

articleTitle: An electronic university: Engineers across the United States can earn master's degrees by enrolling in a new television-based institution
abstract: One of the most unusual universities in the United States is the National Technological University. It has no undergraduate programs, and it does not grant doctorates; it offers only studies leading to the Master of Science degree in various branches of technology. The school's “campus” in Fort Collins, Colo., has only administrative offices. Its faculty reside at universities in nine states, from Alaska to South Carolina. And its students are scattered across the country; few go near a college campus.

articleTitle: The many faces of data vulnerability: Information can be tapped when resident in memory. It can also be intercepted en route, on paper, and elsewhere
abstract: It has been said that we are in a new age - an information age - brought about in large part by the computer and telecommunications. Information is a major commodity: computer security to proton that information has recently been receiving great attention in the public press. However, neither the value of information nor the necessity for its security are new issues.

articleTitle: A new way of managing: Studies comparing U.S. companies with others suggest that U.S. management has failed to grasp that traditional incentives will not motivate an educated work force
abstract: Technology is changing the entire work place, particularly those parts most subject to international competition and to demands for greater productivity and better products an d services. Industrialized countries are shifting from what I call the bureaucratic-industrial system to a new "technoservice" system.

articleTitle: Office routine: The automated pink collar: Secretaries and clerks are often enthusiastic about new technologies, until they discover that shortsighted managers use the new tools to isoiate them further
abstract: Electronic aids are changing work routines in office, but not all changes may be for the better. Studies show that people's work lives must be considered in relation to the new equipment. Otherwise workers can become more disgruntled, even though their initial expectations for the new equipment may have been high.

articleTitle: Lifestyle: Health-care costs: Technology to the rescue? The medical establishment encourages only those new tools that it controls while impeding the implementation of systems that could minimize doctor and hospital costs
abstract: Although there has been a dramatic reduction in deaths from infectious diseases in the last 80 years and though steady gains have been made in containing killer diseases like cancer and heart disease, health care in the United States is falling victim to runaway costs. It has become so expensive that in certain areas of the country the infant mortality rate, due to poverty and limited access to health-care facilities, is still no better than in some undeveloped countries. High costs threaten to undo years of steady progress on the medical front.

articleTitle: Origins of the issues: Theory versus practice, industrial participation, the role of the humanities, and four versus more years are the issues examined
abstract: Technical obsolescence and poor communication skills - the major educational concerns of today's electrical engineer - are far from new issues. They reflect the century-old problem in engineering education: how to provide both a professional and a general education in the “liberal science” undergraduate curriculum of four years. Educators and engineers recognize it as the distinguishing feature between engineering education and professional training in law and medicine. But the problem has been especially apparent in electrical engineering because the vast changes in electrotechnology since the 1880s have continually upset the balance between the electrical engineer's professional and general education. Educators have continually wrestled with such issues as theoretical versus practical training, industrial involvement in education, the value of courses in the humanities and social sciences, and the adequacy of a four-year curriculum.

What one thing more than anything else makes the average electrical engineer happy on the job? Not new technologies, not top equipment, not good hours, not high pay. "By far the moM important factors influencing job satisfaction in the eyes of EEs involve human rdations," according to a key finding of a recent survey in which spectrum, aided by a National Science foundation grant, teamed up with Louis Harris & Associates Inc. to study the job of electrical engineers.

articleTitle: Education: New teacher's pet: The computer: Microcomputers are being imaginatively introduced into liberal-arts curricula, thereby offering hitherto unavailable data and exercises
abstract: Great numbers of students are entering college unversed in mathematics, illiterate in English, and with limited backgrounds In science and a handful of other areas. These problems are well-documented. What is less evident is the way microcomputers are not only helping students offset these problems, but also are improving student learning in a variety of subjects, from business courses to poetry writing.

articleTitle: Japan tests its model communications system: Digital transmission, communications processing, and an innovative bit-based tariff will be studied in the nation's milestone Mitaka plant
abstract: A selected group of about 2000 telephone users, some in downtown Tokyo and some in Mitaka, a suburb of Tokyo, will soon be getting firsthand experience with what may turn out to be their country's communications system in the next century. The project is the Mitaka pilot plant, or Model System, as its creator, the Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Public Corp. (NTT) calls it. It is the largest single project ever undertaken by the NTT and is seen as a milestone in the development of its Information Network System (INS) - an all-digital blend of computer and telecommunications technologies.

The other day I saw "The World of Tomorrow," a documentary film based on the New York World's Fair of 1939–40. The film, currently popular in New York City, consists of newsreels, home movies, and promotional films by Westing-house Electric Corp. and other major exhibitors at the fair.

articleTitle: Lifestyle: Tomorrow's electronic hospital is here today: Computer use is revolutionizing not only hospital laboratories and record-keeping, but also emergency treatment, diagnostics, and intensive care
abstract: Until recently, doctors seeking information on patients at most hospitals had to visit a storage room and pore through files that were hand-written and perhaps intelligible only to their authors. But at state-of-the-art facilities like LDS Hospital of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, doctors need only tap a nearby terminal for patient records. The records are displayed in a clear, standardized format. Moreover, the computer can help the physician interpret the data and even help prescribe appropriate therapy.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: The microprocessor industry shifts from hardware as the driving force in chip design to software, with the widespread acceptance of the UNIX operating system
abstract: Complex microprocessors are now so common that each major manufacturer offers a 32-bit chip. This year, however, the standardization of microprocessor operating systems has eclipsed the new chip introductions. The UNIX operating system, designed in the early 1970s by Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, N.J., was used initially in minicomputers and later in mainframes. It became the virtual standard for 16- and 32-bit microprocessors when Motorola Inc., Intel Corp., National Semiconductor Corp., and Zilog Inc. obtained licenses in May 1983 from the Western Electric Co., which owns the rights to UNIX software, to develop versions of it for their chips.

articleTitle: Frederick E. Terman: Educator and mentor: This popular professor's influence extended far beyond the Stanford University campus; it reached into industry, too
abstract: If a mentor is, as dictionaries suggest, a trusted advisor, teacher, or guide, the late Frederick Emmons Terman of Stanford University was a mentor extraordinary. He once said that he filled the role with encouragement, ideas, and advice. Often he did much more.

articleTitle: Education: `Edutainment' : How to laugh and learn: A grass-roots movement that started in the home is putting school systems under pressure to move computers into the classroom
abstract: A revolution is taking place in the use of computers in learning. But more of the revolution happens to be occurring outside of U.S. educational institutions than inside them. Between 5 and 7 million households now have a personal computer, while about 325 000 are estimated to be in schools. A Gallup Survey found that while 51 percent of personal-computer owners surveyed use the machines to play video games, 46 percent also said that they use them to teach their children spelling ma mathematics.

Tbe question of U.S. preeminence in technology is shifting from the marketplace to the classroom. Product comparisons, highlighting the quality and reliability of U.S. goods versus Japanese goods, for example, are giving way to equally intense discussions about the quality of engineering education in these two countries. Among the major concerns is the question of lifelong learning and which syston better prepares its students for the rigors of ongoing professional development.

articleTitle: EE specialties: Computers are pervasive: Solid-state and computer technologies underlie the shifting emphasis in technical disciplines
abstract: At the turn of the century, the major electrical engineering organization in the United States was the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (AIEE). The Institute of Radio Engineers, the IEEE's other predecessor society, did not yet exist. The membership of the AIEE, which had been founded 16 years earlier, included telegraph operators, inventors, utility-company and electrical-machinery-manufacturing executives, and college physics professors who developed the first rudimentary course in electrical engineering. Some of the AIEE's members called themselves electricians, with a meaning completely foreign to the present-day use of the word.

articleTitle: Software: Progress is reported in expert systems and software to build such systems and in object-oriented programming
abstract: Knowledge systems — artificial-intelligence software capable of giving expert advice or analyzing complex information within particular limited domains - began to reach market in 1983, and further applications are expected this year. Interest in such systems has been spurred by next-generation computing projects in Japan, the United States, and elsewhere, and by the development of low-cost, high-power computers capable of running knowledge-systems software at relatively low cost. (Lisp Machines Inc., Symbolics Inc., and Xerox Corp., for example, are offering computers that run the artificial-intelligence language LISP for $30 000 to $70 000.)

Those of us in the publishing business have a lively interest in the question of whether electronic communication will ever replace the printed word. We know that electronics has gracefully insinuated itself into the front end of the publishing process. We are enthusiastic about that and have spurred the process along as rapidly as we thought appropriate.

What technologies offer the most promising careers to electrical engineers? The current choice of engineers, as revealed in the IEEE Spectrum/Louis Harris survey, could have been surmised from the headlines of major newspapers and magazines: computer software. Seventyfive percent of those queried in the survey rated it among the most promising specialties.

articleTitle: TMI plus 5: Nuclear power on the ropes: The 1979 accident at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant triggered a domino reaction that threatens the future of the U.S. nuclear power industry
abstract: “A serious accident cannot happen.”

articleTitle: Automation in industry: Bleaching the blue collar: Computerization can increase workers' output, but it may also distance product designers from assembly and process requirements
abstract: At first glance, there appears to be an enormous contrast between the Chrysler Corp's Jefferson Avenue plant, an aging assembly facility built in 1907 on Detroit's now deteriorating East Side, and the John Hancock Building, a gleaming glass and steel skyscraper near one of Boston' s poshest neighborhoods. Inside, however, new forms of automation, based on computers and microelectronics, are being used to transform both. At the Jefferson Avenue plant, robots accomplish 98 percent of the welds on new car bodies automatically, while at John Hancock, word processors and other electronic office technologies are laying the basis for a restructured office. The exploding technical capabilities of these new machines and systems, combined in many cases with their plummeting costs, are extending automation to every sector of the economy.

articleTitle: Technology '84 the penetrating technologies: Am analysis by the experts: Taylor L. Booth on computers: Software is the limitation
abstract: In the mid-1980s the computer user is overwhelmed with available hardware. It is software, rather, that has become the limiting factor in computer applications. Each new application seems to specialized software, developed expressly to support it. Unfortunately, software development still resembles a cottage industry in which every new program is painstakingly constructed, strand by strand. The cost of developing the software for a given application is often 10 to 100 times greater than the cost of the hardware on which the software will run.

An engineer who was tmng groomed for a high position in his compmiy sat at his desk in disbelief. Top management had rejected his proposal for installing computers in the manufacturing building. How could the managers fail to understand thm computers would bring efficiency and savings? The old way had worked fine, they said, and besides, the computers would cost too much.

articleTitle: GS/E programs: How to design and apply computers is the objective of a growing class of computer-based curricula that are called by various names
abstract: Most educators agree that the fields of computer hardware and software design are growing and that the number of students being trained for these fields will continue growing with them. But whether these specialists will be called computer engineers, electrical engineers, or computer scientists will probably depend on where they went to school.

articleTitle: TV networks vie for viewer's votes: Sophisticated computer graphics will be the weapons as television technologists compete to speedily convert 1984 election results into exciting home images
abstract: It is 8 p.m. on the east coast of the United States on Nov. 6,1984. The polls have dosed in several states including New Hampshire and Alabama. Correspondents from the three major U.S. television networks stationed at sample precincts in these states are rushing to telephones to report election results to operators at the networks' central computers. The operators key in the results. Each network has 3000 to 4000 sample precincts across the country.

articleTitle: Communicating: Students give oral presentations, create visual aids, and learn engineering by writing
abstract: Engineers have been stereotyped as professionals who are adept at creating and manipulating objects, but who are amateurs at communicating their ideas. Many engineering schools are striving to alter that image.

articleTitle: Technologists and technicians: Two- and four-year programs offer hands-on education in electronics and computers to complement the engineer's skills in activities ranging from research to manufacturing
abstract: Few engineers work ort a shoestring budget, in a small laboratory, and with no supporting personnel. The large size and scope of many electrical engineering projects and organizations call for subdividing engineering tasks. Technicians and others versed more in the practice of engineering concepts than in design and theory are playing important roles. Two- and four-year educational programs have emerged in the last two decades in hundreds of colleges and universities in the United States to provide industry with such a work force. Graduates are grounded in what is called engineering technology, and they are ready, with hands-on experience in electronics and computers, for productive careers in industry. Graduates usually receive more specific training on the job, in programs lasting for from a few weeks to several months.

articleTitle: Technology's global village fragments community life: Transportation and communications technologies widen human horizons but splinter human relationships; computer networks could reverse this trend
abstract: Two hundred years ago, when the United States Constitution was drafted, 90 percent of all work was organized through face-to-face relationships, mostly within the community and family. Small farms predominated. Artisans, working autonomously in their scattered homes and local communities, produced at their own pace, selling not their labor, but a finished product. Since then, the continuing industrial revolution has brought extraordinary increases in productivity to our society, but also a new impersonal scale and a tendency toward economic and political centralization.

articleTitle: Tom L. Powers on communications: VLSI will reduce bandwidth costs and make complex services possible
abstract: The technological trends in the post-Bell-System-divestiture era are clear, although the administrative and political trends may not be. One can readily foresee large national and international call-digital networks in which bandwidth is less and less expensive and software makes complex services possible. Low-cost transmission facilities (via lightwave, satellite, and terrestrial radio relay), advanced software, and incredible amounts of very large-scale integration (VLSI) will make it all possible.

articleTitle: Work: A newsman's view of technology: A prize-winning investigative reporter reflects on his past, when he 'banged out stories' on a manual typewriter, and on how far his profession has come
abstract: In 1968, as a 19-year-old reporter in the so-called Silicon Valley area in northern California, I often interviewed such engineers as Robert Noyee, William Hewlett, and Lester Hogan—as well as philosophers and investors I asked them about the rapidly emerging wonders of the electronic age: computer-calculators that would slip into your pocket, men who soon would walk on the moon, and television and telephone networks that would transform our world into a global village. Then I would rush back to a bureau of the San Jose Mercury News to bang out my stories, using the nineteenth-century mechanical technology of the manual typewriter. My work in those days was more akin to that of reporters who are now a full century into the grave than to what reporters do today, just 16 years later.

articleTitle: Rail transportation: Linear-induction motors, inverters, and microprocessors play a big role in new systems that roll on steel, rubber, or air
abstract: Transit officials of busy cities, constantly searching for new ways to move people quickly, safely, and with reasonable comfort, will be watching closely this year the operation of two new linear-induction motor systems, one in Vancouver, B.C., Canada, and the other in Birmingham, England. The Canadian system has vehicles with wheels that make contact with rails. The English system is using magnetic levitation to raise its vehicles above a rail guideway.

If this special issue of IEEE Spectrum does nothing else, it will underscore the fact that fashions in electrical engineering education change periodically and that fancies are a function of the individual student or professor. In the latter regard we each have our own stories to tell.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Science for life or death
abstract: We notice a continuing schism among engineers concerning the application and control of military technology. Many believe that the engineering community has a special responsibility to instruct and inform the general populace about the potential impact of advanced military technology. Others, even some engaged in developing military systems, believe that “engineers should engineer” and that the use of military technology should be left up to our democratic political system.“We have no business interfering where we have no competence,” they assert.

articleTitle: The cat battery: Ill-starred and short-lived
abstract: This 100-year-old development had been little publicized. Oddly, the science editor of Life magazine was the first, in 1884, to write about its theory and application

articleTitle: Scarce programs: From power engineering and electromagnetics to telecommunications and instrumentation, specialized programs are in short supply
abstract: Technical managers in industry in the united States seeking to hire engineers who are well-versed in six disciplines may have fewer graduates to choose from than they would like. For different reasons, each of these disciplines - power engineering, electromagnetics, instrumentation, computer networking in telecommunications, manufacturing engineering, and the application of engineering to public policymaking - fails to meet industry demands for qualified engineers. The shortage is reflected in many statements made by industry managers in recent meetings, panel discussions, and symposia.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The issues we avoid
abstract: We engineers and other technical professionals are not noted for our involvement in nontechnical activities—whether they be at local or global levels. There are probably several reasons for this. Even in school our interests are usually more narrowly focused on those courses we deem of immediate importance and usefulness. We are not noted for our communication and human-relations skills. And, like the rest of the populace, our interest in certain issues flags when times are good.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Industry offers a pragmatic alternative to the dearth of academic programs
abstract: Instrumentation is a broad field, encompassing a broad spectrum of engineering and scientific disciplines. But there is a dearth of colleges and universities at which the subject can be studied in depth. “If you want to do graduate work in instrumentation” said William D. Walker, president and chief executive officer of Electro-Scientific Industries Inc. of Portland, Ore., “then go to work for Hewlett-Packard or Tektronix.”

articleTitle: Before electronics: Room for error: Computer graphics has revolutionized television studios
abstract: Before 1972, getting the results of the November elections to the home-television viewer was largely a mechanical activity, with sometimes inaccurate and perhaps boring results. In the early 1960s TV studios that broadcast the election results resembled small-town ballparks. Races were listed on large boards with slots for numbers. Fifty or more human pages ran around the boards trying to put the numbers in the right slot.

articleTitle: Manufacturing: Computer applications in the factory spur corresponding efforts in the university
abstract: When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first space satellite, in 1957, it put intense pressure on the United States to bolster education in engineering and science. One result was an increased emphasis on science in engineering programs.

articleTitle: Company D: A fortress undisturbed: Here the research engineers are well insulated from distracting pressures and free to pursue their interests. But is the real world too remote?
abstract: This is the fifth article in the Spectrum series on electrical-engineering work environments and the bench-level and managing engineers who work in them. Four companies-manufacturers of semiconductors, computers, military equipment, and consumer products - are the focus of the study. All were guaranteed anonymity in exchange for granting Spectrum freedom in interviewing and observing their employees at work.

articleTitle: Societal awareness: Programs stress the interaction of engineering, environmental issues, and policy
abstract: The age of activism is in full swing, No longer do consumers accept technological advances at face value; they want to know what effect each will have on society and the environment. Such questions have made it urgent for scientists and engineers to become knowledgeable about the interaction between science, technology, and society. “I think we have to teach students how to deal with this kind of ambiguity because that's what their lives have to deal with,” said Walter R. Lynn, director of the science, technology, and society program at Cornell university.

articleTitle: A guide to school guides: Selecting the right college or graduate program is aided by both traditional references and emerging computer programs
abstract: Choosing a college or graduate program ranks as one of life's most important decisions. For students with a technical bent the choice is particularly crucial, because a school with a good overall reputation may prove inadequate in engineering or science.

articleTitle: Whatever happened to the tunnel diode?
Company C: Quiescent and secure: Engineers here love security and this company provides that. But does security make for a lean and hungry organization?
abstract: This is the fourth article in the Spectrum series on engineering work environments and the bench-level and managing engineers that work in them. four companies - manufacturers of semiconductors, computers, military equipment, and consumer products - are the focus on the study. All were guaranteed anonymity in exchange for granting freedom in interviewing and observing their employees at work.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The joys and hazards of looking ahead
abstract: 1984. It's here. George Orwell, painting a picture of a perverted society based on a projection of a centralized economy that had "already been partly realized in Communism and Fascism" in his day, objected when readers interpreted his satirical novel as a forecast. "I do not believe that the kind of society I describe necessarily will arrive, but I believe ... that something resembling it could arrive."

articleTitle: Model programs: There is a smorgasbord of offerings from universities, industry, professional societies, and commercial firms
abstract: Engineers at a newly divested West Coast telephone company begin pressuring their managers to develop a program that will help them move confidently into modern telecommunications.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Opening a time capsule
abstract: Many readers may recall the muck, "Ten vignettes of an engineering institute," published in the 1976 special IEEE Proceedings issue titled "Two centuries in retrospect," a celebration of the U.S. Bicentennial. The article was written by Ivan S. Coggeshall, IEEE Fellow and former president of the Institute of Radio Engineers. There were few members in 1976 who were as qualified to write such an article and there are even fewer today. "Coggie" began his career as a counter clerk and Morse student with the Postal Telegraph-Cable Co. of Newport, R.I., in 1912. By 1920 he had become an engineering assistant in Western Union's New York Office of the Vice President in Charge of Traffic and thereupon rose steadily in the ranks of Western Union to director of international communications in 1957 and assistant vice president in 1959.

articleTitle: James M. Early on solid state: The theoretical ideals come ever closer
abstract: Digital techniques reign supreme in solid-state technology. Integrated-circuit chips use digital pulse-code modulation to make possible new levels of performance in electronic equipment, switching power supplies use pulse-width modulation to save power and cut power loss, and image sensors use pulse-amplitude modulation to convert variable light patterns into a stream of pulses.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Technology transfer at issue
abstract: Some problems have to permanent solutions. Controlling the transfer of militarily useful technology over international borders is one of them. Admiral Bobby Inman expressed it well when he said, "There is an overlap between technological information and national security which produces tension. This tension results from the scientists' desire for unconstrained research and publication on the one hand and the Federal government's need to protect certain information from potential foreign adversaries who might use that information against this nation. Both are powerful forces." The task, Adm. Inamn said, is finding a workable and just balance between them.

articleTitle: Education: How technology influences journalism: Minicameras and microwave dishes have facilitated the gathering and transmission of news, but have the city editors and TV news producers raised the quality of the product they deliver?
abstract: News is a strange product. It is a shaper of society—essential in a democratic process that depends on an informed public. It is a highly profitable commodity in a multibillion-dollar industry. But it is also a technological artifact.

articleTitle: Industrial electronics: Precision robots, vision systems, and expert systems intensify the computer's role on the production floor
abstract: Many manufacturing process are becoming more dependent on computers, and with good reason. Computer-controlled robots can now assemble up to 15 components per minute on a printed-circuit beard with 25-micrometer precision, a thing unheard of only a few years ago.

articleTitle: Photo-Electric 100: Winners of the IEEE Spectrum Centennial photography contest
abstract: Through sponsorship of the Photo-Electric 100 contest Spectrum sought to illuminate twin themes of the IEEE's 100th anniversary; the human richness of electrical engineering's past and the profound variety of its present. The contest was announced in the June 1983 issue of Spectrum. Its themes were represented by a pair of contest categories. One challenged contestants to capture some aspea of modem electrotechnology in their own photographs. The other covered historical photographs, whether or not taken by the entrant. Judges were professional photographers Steve Eisenberg (who created the cover for the June issue of Spectrum) and Michael Hirst, along vnth historians Robert Friedel and Joyce E. Bedi of the IEEE Center for the History of Electrical Engineering. In addition to those photographs selected by the judges for prkes and honorable mentions, five entries were recognized by Spectrum with an Editor's Special Award. The Grand Award winners received $1000 each. Second- and third-place winners received camera equipment contributed by Olympus Corp.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: New audio and video developments await their true test in the marketplace; software support may make the difference
abstract: In the ever-expanding consumer-electronics market, 1983 was a year of high promise and dashed hopes. Sales of television sets spurted with the emergence of higher-quality monitors - some included as part of component systems - and the first steps toward high-definition telecasting were taken.

articleTitle: Education: Education initiatives by states, industry, and the Federal government may not help schools that need them most
abstract: A variety of programs were started in 1983 to counter what many educators consider a crisis in engineering education. Some engineering deans, however, worry that state and industry initiatives are benefiting a relatively small group of already healthy schools. If the actions of the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET) in the last year are any indication, the health of engineering education in the United States is bad and getting worse. The board, which is charged by 20 engineering societies with setting and enforcing standards in U.S. engineering schools, granted the maximum six-year term of accreditation to only 35 percent of the programs it reviewed last year, down three percentage points from 1982, and 23 points from 1978. The numbers of schools that did not meet the board's minimum standards in 1982-83 increased to 9 percent, up from 5 percent in 1982.

articleTitle: Aerospace and military: A new space communications satellite, demonstrations of the MX missile, and infrared mapping are highlighted
abstract: Aerospace and military projects made impressive and often spectacular gains in 1983, but they also had a number of snags. Flights of the U.S. Space Shuttle were delayed because of cracked fuel manifolds and faulty rocket insulation, among other things. The malfunctioning of a U.S. Air Force rocket hampered deployment of a new space-communications system. And a chief component of a military infrared avionics system is being side. stepped while the rest of the system began testing.

Our profession has created a veritable glut of records and artifacts including research notebooks, proposals, memos, and the like—not to mention a plethora of mock-ups, breadboards, models, and eouipment prototypes. And both are increasing at an exponential rate. Which documents and hardware should be saved? And for what purposes?

articleTitle: Electromagnetics: Industrial demand spawns a `renaissance ' in an established discipline
abstract: An upsurge in demand throughout the United States for engineers specializing in electromagnetics is putting heavy pressure on universities and industry to expand educational programs in this area. The Hughes Aircraft Co. in El Segundo, Calif., alone says it needs more than 120 such engineers this year and a similar number next year. And on the East Coast, the Raytheon Co. of Bedford, Mass., is planning to recruit scores of microwave specialists in the next few years.

Medicine, law, engineering —all ihe great professions —began as needed arts or crafts. Their evolution makes it impossible to identify a particular day, or even a year, when they emerged ns full-blown kearfied pursuits. In the case of electrical engineering, however, one could make a good case for May 13, 1884, as the day the profession was formalized—at least in the United States. On that date, Thomas Alva Edison and Alexander Grahmn Bell met with five colleagues and formed the America institute of Electrical Engineers, which in 1963 merged with the younger institute of Radio Engineers to become today's IEEE.

articleTitle: Telecommunications: Digital communications and computer science are combined into popular programs
abstract: The invention of the microprocessor in 1971 opened the floodgates of what had previously been a contained discipline: computer science. Computers now pervade most electrical engineering disciplines, but few more than telecommunications. It has evolved in the past decade from the point-to-point communication of computers to the linking of computers into networks.

articleTitle: Do EE careers suffer from poor management?
abstract: This is the concluding article in the Spectrum series of six on engineering work environments and the bench-level and managing engineers that work in them. Four companies - manufacturers of computers, semiconductors, military equipment, and consumer products and referred to in previous articles as Companies A through D. respectively - were the focus of the study. Alt were guaranteed anonymity in exchange for granting Spectrum permission to interview and observe their employees at work.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Nuclear trials and tribulations
abstract: Events at two nuclear power stations - one operational and the other awaiting licensing - illustrate the range of problems facing the nuclear industry in the United States today. The morass encompasses technical, economic, and political issues - one inseparable from the others.

articleTitle: Television graphics hardware: Speed is the key: Up to 2 megabytes must be manipulated within 1/30 of a second
abstract: Unlike the systems that generate computer graphic images for movies and commercials - and take hours to generate each frame - the hardware used to generate or manipulate television images must, above ail else, be fast. Speed is the designer's major criterion in selecting the microprocessors and memories that go into the systems.

articleTitle: Wescon '84: Focus on local area networks: New standards for LANs- and ways of conforming to them - are a prime topic at the Anaheim, Calif., meeting Oct. 30-Nov. 2
abstract: Science fiction mem science fact at Wescon '84 when Ray Bradbury marks the IEEE's first 100 years at a celebration banquet on Nov. 1. Mr. Bradbury, author of over 400 short stories and 17 novels, including Fahrenheit 451, The Illustrated Man, and The Martian Chronicles, will review a century of progress in electrical engineering and speculate on process over the next 100 years.

articleTitle: What is due the engineer? Why do U.S. engineers have little influence, while Japanese engineers head many companies and Soviet engineers end up in the Politburo?
abstract: The plane has just landed at the airport. It's your first trip to Latin America. The driver who has been sent to pick you up addresses you as "In-geniero." It is the first time anyone has addressed you by title, and surprise quickly gives way to pleasure. Engineers are addressed by title in Latin America, in Europe, and in most other parts of the world, except Great Britain and the United States. It is a symbol of recognition and respect, but more than that it is a clue to the high status that engineers enjoy.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Through the looking glass
abstract: The Long Island Lighting Co. (Lilco), a private investor-owned utility, on Jan. 10 notified Suffolk County, N.Y., in which its nearly complete Shoreham nuclear power station is located, that it would withheld $26.2 million in real-estate taxes. The Lilco directors took the step both as a protest of the assessment on the plant and in response to Suffolk County's opposition to allowing it to operate.

articleTitle: Electro, '84: Memories and more: An outstanding professional program, tutorial seminars, and exhibits will greet attendees of the May electronics convention in Boston
abstract: Electro '84 will combine with the IEEE Centennial anniversary and the Mini-Micro Northeast Conference for a week-long industry event in Boston in mid-May. Thc annual IEEE electronics convention and exhibition will be held May 15-17, as will the Mini-Micro show. The IEEE Centennial events will start on Sunday, May 13.

To produce this annual remew of eiecirotechnoiogy. IEEE Spectrum's editors called upon a broad range of experts - some 120 in all. Ronald K. Jurgen, IEEE Specturm's administrative editor and coordinator of The issue, began tlie process of contacting experts, many of them representatives of the IEEE's own Technical Societies, about six months ago. The finished report iepresents an attempt io identify significant trends and to provide tixampies by citing specific hardware and/or software by name and manufactiirer wherever appropriate.

articleTitle: Centennial hall of fame: Today's electrical engineers select the major contributors - Technical, industrial, and academic - to the profession and society
Fabrication: chip fabricators run the `anchor leg′ in producing a complex chip in the allotted time: they begin on day 15 and finish on day 31
abstract: Major changes will be needed in widely accepted fabrication practices to make the one-month chip a feasible attainment throughout the semiconductor industry. That fabricators can do the job in the two weeks allotted to them - chip design accounts for the first two weeks -is already being demonstrated by some chip manufacturers.

articleTitle: Robert A. Bell on power and energy: Uncertainties and perceptions of risk bold back energy technology exploitation
abstract: The continuing loss of momentum of energy-related research, along with its many long-term strategic implications, continues to be a disturbing trend in the United States. Significant reductions in Federally supported short-term research programs have placed many new burdens on industry's already strained resources. Directions of energy research seem to reflect the turbulence resulting from an important shift away from the goal of energy independence. Nevertheless many admirable projects are under way: fuel cells, fluidized-bed coal combustion, magnetohydrodynamics, nuclear fusion, and photovoltaics are examples; and important progress is being made.

articleTitle: Business outlook: Design work stations, silicon foundries, and a DOD communications network presage a fundamental alteration of the semiconductor industry
abstract: The semiconductor industry is about to undergo sweeping change. The development in the last few years of relatively inexpensive IC-design work stations and the emergence of silicon foundries-a new kind of company devoted to making chips fast-are expected to alter drastically the traditional roles of the semiconductor supplier and hardware maker. Burgeoning demand for the design and fabrication of chips in one month is expected. With the recent opening to the commercial world of ARPAnet, a communications network run by the U.S. Defense Department, the basic ingredients to realize the one-month chip are now in place: speedy design, with the aid of both work stations and ARPAnet, and fast fabrication at specialized foundries.

articleTitle: Company B: The competitive edge: Ambition and aggression are the keys to getting ahead. Are technical talents being wasted in the clash?
abstract: This is the third article in the Spectrum series on engineering work environments and the bench-level and managing engineers that work in them. Four companies - manufacturers of semiconductors, computers, military equipment, and consumer products - are the focus of the study. All were guaranteed anonymity in exchange for freedom in interviewing and observing their employees at work.

In a recent issue of Chemtech, the results of an opinion survey of chemical engineers conducted during what we suspect may have been a fictitious meeting of the American Chemical Society were presented. Also, the methodology through which a responsible, respectable, and representative sample was achieved was described: "...only members of the society over 50 years of age who voted for Reagan in 1980 were asked to participate. Respondents were asked to check those words on [a] list that they felt applied to all splendid scientists (i.e., those most like themselves). To avoid any bias whatsoever, the inquiry was conducted on a double-blind basis: the [pollsters] subjected themselves to a high-alcohol-content diet for three days prior to the experiment, and each respondent was required to consume a minimum of one double martini before his responses were recorded." The authors concluded that, beyond question, the poll "demonstrated that chemists, if not actually better than all other human beings, are, to say the least, a credit to their race and a damned fine group of upstanding and patriotic Americans, all of whom embody the finest attributes that can be attributed to those to whom those attributes can be attributed."*

articleTitle: Instrumentation: VLSI chips present new challenges for testing, while personal computers and local networks lead to new approaches
abstract: Test and measurement equipment responded last year both to the new technologies under test and to the changing test engineer's tools. Some advances involved the introduction of completely new equipment, others the reconfiguring of the familiar or the improving of the conventional.

articleTitle: Education: Bringing learning home: Instructional TV: New experiments with television as a teaching medium are promising a democratization of learning beyond even that accomplished by the public schools
abstract: The invention of movable type and the printing press by Johann Gutenberg, a mechanical revolution in education, extended access to knowledge stored in print from elite scholars and scribes to the masses. This, in turn, gave rise to universal literacy and the establishment of public schools for education. But the growth in applications of electronic technologies may have an even more rapid and democratic effect than the public schools have had. It will extend formal learning beyond the classroom into the home and work place.

articleTitle: Gems from the Smithsonian: From its collection of more than 17 000 historical electrical and electronic artifacts, the curator of the Smithsonian's electrical section selected these as seminal
abstract: In 1846, when the Smithsonian Institution was officially established, Joseph Henry was named its first secretary-a position he held for more than three decades. During that time Henry did ml encourage the development of a museum, believing that the very limited resources of the privately endowed fledgling organization should be alocated to scientific research. But he understood the value of displaying the artifacts of science as a way to improve public understanding and stimulate an interest in science among young people. So when Congress appropriated funds in the 1850s to support museum activities, Henry not only allowed his own apparatus to be displayed, but he also encouraged some of his friends to donate similar items.

articleTitle: Making computers think like people [fuzzy set theory]
abstract: Attempts to automate various types of human activity, from assembling an automobile to diagnosing a patient, have often been impeded by the gap between the way humans reason and the way computers are generally programmed. When making decisions, computers usually ask questions that have a clear-cut yes or no answer: “Does the temperature exceed 75.6°?” “Is Mary older than John?” Humans don't generally reason in such a precise manner. Rather, most human thinking deals with categories that shade into one another: “it's dangerous to drive on a very icy road” or “A complex circuit must be designed for high reliability.”

articleTitle: The hemt: A superfast transistor: An experimental GaAs-AlGoAs device switches in picoseconds and generates little heat. This is just what supercomputers need
abstract: A new transistor is being born in laboratories around the world, the fastest yet. It switches on or off in only slightly more than 10 picoseconds. It functions not only as a digital switch, but can also serve as an analog amplifier at frequencies up to about 60 gigahertz.

articleTitle: The trials of wafer-scale integration: Although major technical problems have been overcome since WSI was first tried in the 1960s, commercial companies can't yet make it fly
abstract: The superchips are coming! Units under development in industrial and academic laboratories both in the United States and Japan will integrate millions of logic gates into a single package the size of a man's hand. Ultimately, the circuits will encompass an entire wafer. In this size the superchips may be termed wafer-scale integrated (WSI) systems.

articleTitle: Cryptology and the origins of spread spectrum: Engineers during World War II developed an unbreakable scrambler to guarantee secure communications between Allied leaders; actress Hedy Lamarr played a role in the technology
abstract: Deep in the guarded labyrinth of the newly constructed Pentagon, an army lieutenant with top security clearance inserts a voltohmmeter probe into a horse-shoe-shaped, 7-foot-high panel of electronic equipment. The apparatus is top secret; the room where it sits, with its polished tile floor, is windowless.

articleTitle: Design case history: Apple's Macintosh: A small team of little-known designers, challenged to produce a low-cost, exceptionally easy-to-use personal computer, turns out a technical milestone
abstract: In 1979 the Macintosh personal computer existed only as the pet idea of Jef Raskin, a veteran of the Apple II team, who had proposed that Apple Computer Inc. make a low-cost “appliance” type computer that would be as easy to use as a toaster. Mr. Raskin believed the computer he envisioned, which he called Macintosh, could sell for $1000 if it was manufactured in high volume and used a powerful microprocessor executing tightly written software.

articleTitle: Nuclear-electric power in space: Nuclear-reactor power systems could produce an abundance of new applications in space, hut design hurdles abound
abstract: The chief power sources being used today in space " solar arrays, fuel cells, and radioisotope generators " will be inadequate for many, more ambitious future space missions. Compact, lightweight power systems, yet to be developed, that can produce up to 1000 kilowatts of electric power (kWe) will eventually be needed and three U.S. government agencies believe the solutions is to develop a system based on nuclear energy.

articleTitle: Smart credit cards: The answer to cashless shopping: Pioneered in France, microprocessor-based credit and debit cards are being used in large-scale tests in three cities there
abstract: You walk over to a special pay phone in a large airport, insert your electronic-communication services card, and enter your password. The telephone acknowledges that a central computer has validated your identity by flashing a service menu on the luminescent screen. You choose from “Local directories,” “Long-distance directories,” “Personal directory,” “Rates,” “Place call,“ and “Information services.“ You press the number for “Personal directory,” and the screen changes to a numbered listing of a dozen names and telephone numbers drawn from your card's memory. You punch in 9 for a certain friend's number, and the screen dissolves into a pricing and payment schedule: TOLL CALL. 75 cents for the first three minutes, 10 cents each additional minute.

articleTitle: Can computer crime be stopped? The proliferation of microcomputers in today's information society has brought with it new problems in protecting both computer systems and their resident intelligence
abstract: A police officer in New York City stopped a car that went through a red light. Inside was a suitcase containing $1 million worth of payroll checks - the profits of a computer crime that had yet to be discovered by its victim.

articleTitle: The wired university: In a growing number of institutions, educators are integrating powerful personal computers and networks into a new learning environment
abstract: A rapidly expanding group of engineering educators is adopting the view that their students must have wide access to powerful computing facilities. One reason for this view is that computers are becoming pervasive in the engineering work place, and students must be prepared for a smooth transition to professional practice. A second, more important reason for giving students the widest possible access to powerful computing facilities is that computers can enhance the learning process: by making new tools available to students, they can improve both problem-solving skills and understanding; and by increasing the “intellectual leverage” of teachers and researchers, they can aid in the creation and dissemination of new knowledge.

articleTitle: Semiconductor optical amplifiers: Beyond their role as transmitters in fiber-optic systems, laser diodes can be made to amplify light, perhaps promising simple all-optical repeaters
abstract: Part of the original vision of integrated optics is the ultimate creation of a fiber-optic system that would be a complete optical analog to traditional electronic systems. In such a system the light, once generated, would not only be transmitted optically, but would also be amplified optically and received by direct optical detection.

articleTitle: Biological effect of electromagnetic fields: New findings linking changes in organisms to irradiation by weak fields encourage researchers to posit theories, although research is incomplete
abstract: In the past three years, the study of the biological effects of radio-frequency electromagnetic (EM) fields has taken a new turn. At the beginning of the 1980s, researchers still argued about whether all effects of fields on organisms were caused simply by the heating induced by intense radiation or if some effects also occurred at field strengths too low to produce even localized heating. Although laboratory results had by that time convinced some researchers that athermal effects-those that could not be explained by heating - did in fact occur, a vocal group of scientists still doubted that these laboratory results were valid and repeatable.

articleTitle: Data-flow architecture: A decentralized structure based on the flow of data will permit future computers to operate at even higher speeds
abstract: The development of a new generation of faster, more intelligent computers " the goal of major projects in the United States, Japan, and Europe " requires not Only the perfection of faster devices but also new ways of linking chips. In the view of many computer scientists, the key to obtaining much higher speeds is the abandonment of the conventional Von Neumann architecture and the adoption of new designs, in which calculations are performed in parallel rather than in a fixed sequence.

articleTitle: Photovoltaic-cell technologies joust for position: The fabrication of solar cells has become a bona fide industry with three versions vying to dominate the marketplace
abstract: After two decades of trial and error, many researchers believe that photovoltaic cells - which convert light into electric current - are fast approaching the time when they will be ready for widespread use. Cell efficiencies have improved to the point where modules are a competitive energy source for users not connected to a utility grid. By the turn of the century, sanguine researchers predict, photovoltaics will be a cheaper source of electricity than oil. Until recently the application of photovoltaic cells has been confined to power source for spacecraft and remote communication devices, and some limited home use.

articleTitle: Teleconferencing comes of age: Electronic meetings enter a new era, thanks to personal computers, video printers, slide projectors, and bright graphics, among other tools
abstract: It is 9 a.m. in New York, 2 p.m. in London, and an important teleconference is about to begin between a corporate headquarters in New York and the company's branch in London. More than a dozen executives and their staffs gather at each end to confer conveniently using high-quality audio and visual fidelity.

articleTitle: The origins of EE education: a matter of degree
abstract: As the 1830s began, Thomas Alva Edison had big plans - and problems. His new light was becoming his new system. Indeed, the entire incandescent lighting system was already a fait accompli in the minds of many. Although the Pearl Street Station in New York- the first enterprise offering to sell incandescent lighting to the public-would not open until September 1882. Edison was busy installing isolated lighting plants. As early as February 1881, builders in cities such as Chicago and Boston were wiring new structures for the electric lights that they were sure would come. The great Paris Electrical Exhibition of 1881 gave the world a taste of the future, and one of the foremost exhibits was Edison's system - dynamo, lamp, conductors, and switches.

articleTitle: The drive to regulate electromagnetic fields: In the United States, states and localities are imposing regulations, and industry is seeking action by the Federal government
abstract: A few years ago, the electronics and communications industries were more than content that, in the United States, there were no compulsory regulations limiting human exposure to electromagnetic (EM) fields. In the view of many industry spokesmen, the dangers of such fields were minimal in any case. Today many corporations and trade groups, ranging from broadcasters to radar manufacturers, are urgently demanding that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) or some other national agency set up standards.

articleTitle: A survey of color graphics printing: User needs for permanent copies of charts, graphs, and other illustrations are growing rapidly, and the technology is catching up to meet the demand
abstract: Electronic color printers may be novelties today, but they are headed for explosive growth on a broad front in corning years because of the convergence of several technological trends: rising demand for color graphics in computer work stations, advances In printing technologies, and a boom in office automation, Although the demand for color printers is now only a fraction of that for black and white printers, it is increasing at a faster rate, doubling each year. A vast number of potential users with a broad spectrum of applications for color hard copy remain to be tapped.

articleTitle: Testing: Previously the most neglected area, chip testing must begin during the chip-design phase and continue through fabrication
abstract: Designing and fabricating a very large-scale integrated chip in one month is pointless if the chip does not work. Yet methods of testing such a chip quickly and cheaply have received scant attention until recently, test engineers say. The area has suffered from both a lack of understanding by engineering managers of the importance of testing and a lack of computer tools to help the test engineer design test programs. The technologies for rapid design and fabrication of custom chips have far outpaced the technology of testing.

articleTitle: Technology as a tool for teaching EEs: As electrical engineering departments become even more computerized, colleges will admit more students and employ innovative techniques for teaching them
abstract: A slow but certain change is taking place in the teaching of electrical engineering. It is part of a broad change in U.S. higher education: an electronic university is beginning to emerge. Many components have been develops and are akeady in place-personal computers, computer-controlled video-disk systems, and video cassette recorders. Only cost and convenience will dictate if the changeover to an electronic university occurs on a wide scale in one decade, two decades, or more. But already private enterprise has jumped into the breach.

articleTitle: The new television: Looking behind the tube: The viewer gets a host of new options with the advent of new frequency allocations. The likely impact on the traditional broadcaster is discussed in this first part of a two-part series
abstract: Nations around the world are gearing up for the greatest explosion in television technology since the earliest days of broadcasting three to four decade ago. In the United States, recent rulings of the Federal Communications Commission, coupled with advances in technology, have opened up new portions of the electromagnetic spectrum to television programming. Moreover, the FCC has also repealed restrictions that prevented other regions of the spectrum from being fully developed.

articleTitle: More electronics in Detroit's 1985 models: Bells and whistles take a hack seat to functional, efficient design and to the integration of instrumentation
abstract: After years of experience with electronic devices and systems in cars, automobile manufacturers are moving toward a more mature, integrated-systems approach to design. For example, in some 1985 cars microprocessors communicate with each other, sharing input data, to provide more precise control of car functions. Single instruments are programmed to give multiple readouts. And instruments, on-board diagnostics, and navigational systems are designed to share one overall display.

articleTitle: On the horizon: Fast chips quickly: It's done using silicon compilers. Though they've built some significant circuits, their mare ambitious roles are still in the future
abstract: Imagine the following scene. A physicist in need of some special signal-processing chips for a particle-physics experiment goes to a computer terminal and, over a network, accesses a silicon compiler. The physicist specifies the functions the chip is to perform - perhaps data selection, followed by a series of complex transformations, ending with conversion to a standard data format for further processing and analysis (as is done by very large-scale computers in present-day particle physics). The compiler verifies that specified operations applied to imputs with the bit width chosen will give rise to the correct-size outputs. catches a logic error in the data-selection specifications by checking them against the expected properties of the outputs, checks that the algorithm specified by the physicist will work efficiently on silicon, and goes off to compile the chip. A day later, the physicist is informed - probably by electronic mail over the same network used to access the compiler - that the circuit has been designed; it will occupy a 400-by-500-mil area using 1-micrometer design rules. The note adds that it has been placed into the fabrication queue at a nearby silicon foundry and will be ready in four weeks.

articleTitle: Solid state: Memories amass more data per chip, while several companies ready the first nonoptical lithography machines
abstract: Historically the semiconductor industry was primarily a U.S. industry. By the end of 1982, however, Japan had secured 35 percent of the world market, compared with 55 percent for the United States. Much of the increase, and most of Japan's growth in 1983, came from sales of 64-kilobit random-access memories: approximately two thirds of those sold so far have been made by Japanese companies. In September 1983, however, a U.S. company grabbed the semiconductor headlines when the IBM Corp. announced an experimental 512-kb RAM with the greatest storage capacity on a RAM chip yet retorted.

articleTitle: Propelling passengers fester than a speeding Bullet: As maglev urban railways get tracking, lines in West Germany, Japan, and Canada are expected to follow England's commercial lead
abstract: In May. magnetic-levitation cars began carrying passengers between the airport at Birmingham, England, and that city's International Railway Station and the adjacent British National Exhibition Centre. The 625-meter-long route is the first of several urban maglev railways that will begin commercial service in the next few years. By next year, for example, maglev cars wil begin operation on a 1.6-kilometer guideway in West Berlin, which will link a subway station with a zoo and cultural center.

articleTitle: EEs on lifelong learning: A survey of readers indicate how they keep current, assess recent learning experiences, and rate course topics
abstract: Without continual updating of their education, electrical engineers are prone to wind up on a technical scrap heap, pushed to the periphery as new fields and newly trained engineers emerge. But there appears to be growing recognition among industry, Government, and university officials in the United States that engineers represent a valuable resource that should not be allowed to “depreciate” so rapidly as technology advances.

articleTitle: EE education around the world: The educational systems of the United States, the Soviet Union, Japan, West Germany, France, the United Kingdom, and India are compared
abstract: Engineering education in most technologically advanced countries is in a period of intense reexamination. In the United States there has been growing concern that engineering schools are graduating too few Ph.D.s to fill the needs of industry and defense, as well as to replenish the ranks of university faculties, and that secondary schools are not preparing the general population properly in science and mathematics. In Japan, where science and math training are emphasized in secondary schools, industrial leaders are asking if the universities are encouraging the creativity needed to move Japan from the role of rapid adapter and improver of the technologies developed by other countries to that of technological leader. In the Soviet Union, government officials have questioned the excessive narrowness of its engineering education and the inadequacy of part-time courses. In France, there is concern that engineering schools are attracting too many bright students for management programs, leaving only less able students for scientific research.

articleTitle: A review of engineering workstations: These powerful computers are to the engineer what word processors are to the secretary: No panacea, hut an important aid
abstract: Engineering workstations for electronic design - I desktop computer systems almost as powerful as a traditional minicomputer - have generated considerable excitement in the past two years. With their I high-resolution graphic displays, they are intended to fill the engineer's need for sketch pad, bread-1 board, calculator, and almost anything else. Engineering workstations can potentially be used to speed every facet of the design engineer's job, from refining an initial concept to beginning full production. Are these very expensive new tools fulfilling their promise?

articleTitle: EE careers: New directions but old issues: To manage or not to manage, how to avoid obsolescence, how to maintain the joy of creating- The old debates haven't slackened as EES enter their second century
abstract: As electrical engineering enters its second century the profession is, by many indicators, in better shape than ever. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has projected that over half a million more engineering jobs will open up in the next decade. Antitechnology sentiments of the 1960s have waned; the public is enamored of electronics.

articleTitle: Lifestyle: Mythinformation in the high-tech era: The romanticization of the personal computer as a social panacea threatens to blind society to the fact that without guiding wisdom even the best tool can be misused
abstract: "[With powerful personal computers] revolution, transformation and salvation are all to be carried out."

articleTitle: High-tech batteries for power utilities: Load leveling and peak shaving are attractive reasons for power companies and customers alike to encourage development of advanced batteries
abstract: As electric utilities respond to mounting pressures to provide electricity more efficiently, reliably, and cheaply, they may in the near future be turning to one of the oldest electrical devices: the storage battery. A far cry from Volta's pile, the batteries under development for utility applications will eventually store megawatthours of energy.

articleTitle: Medical ultrasonics: As new techniques are perfected, ultrasound extends its usefulness from diagnosis to research, therapy, and even surgery
abstract: One of the most widely used electronic techniques in medicine today is ultrasound. Physicians using it can now measure the velocity of blood flow in high-risk pregnancies; examine the brains of newborn babies; take motion pictures of a patient's heart; and detect cancerous tumors and the plaques in blood vessels that cause arteriosclerosis. In obstetrics the use of ultrasound has become routine; it is believed that today as many as 40 percent of pregnant women in the United States have at least one such scan.

Most of us have visited recreations of early American homes in such places as Williamsburg, Va., and Sturbridge Village, Mass. They convey a feeling of barrenness, an evocation of a life consumed with work and struggle. Enter-tainment had no place. The furnishings were forbidding, and there was little reading material. Could one piece of modern electrotechnology transform the most inhospitable of these dwellings? Is there any doubt it would be a television set? Even in the present-day slums, television sets are an overwhelming choice before such seeming necessities as refrigerators and telephones.

articleTitle: Design: Chip designers are allocated 14 working days to complete their part of the team effort; they must rely on scare, expensive software tools
abstract: Designers face mixed prospects in helping to develop on integrated-circuit chip in one month. Enough automated software tools are commercially available to help them do the job in 14 days, the deadline they must meet. Those tools, however, are expensive and in some cases hard to get. Furthermore, the limited performance of most tools today imposes certain constraints on the complexity, density, and performance of the chip.

articleTitle: Maintenance proctors for mainframe computer: Special-purpose computers supervise the proper operation of their host computer to improve reliability and reduce down time
abstract: As computers become faster and more complex, their application in government, industry, and science is becoming so critical that users can no longer afford the luxury of down time when something goes wrong with the machine. Long waits for technicians to arrive, troubleshoot the system, and repair or replace parts are no longer acceptable; reliability and maintenance must be built in. In small computer systems, this is being done with redundant hardware and software. But in large mainframe machines, the cost of redundant hardware is too high to the cost-effective except for certain specialized applications. Instead, fault tolerance has been achieved by the development of specialized computers that keep watch on what the main processor is doing, diagnose faults when they occur, and take corrective action that would be difficult or impossible for the main processor alone. These specialized computers are called maintenance processors.

articleTitle: Technology '84 personal computers: Common sense replaces computerese, steps are taken toward standardization, and interactive graphics gains ground
abstract: Personal computers have grown in the last few years from vehicles for video games and word processing into machines rivaling minis and mainframes in computing power. The personal computers introduced last year, however, are marked not only by this characteristic but by a new emphasis on sophisticated software and graphics. The user no longer gains access to the computer's power only by typing cryptic code words through a keyboard but also by pointing to symbols on a screen; he can use common sense rather than computerese. A variety of different approaches, combining graphics software and hardware, are seen in new products: screen cursors controlled with a joystick or a “mouse,” touch screens, graphic “windows,“ and programmable, or “soft,” keys.

articleTitle: The new television: Looking behind the tube: In this second part of a two-part series, the outlook for emerging direct-broadcast satellite technology and entrenched cable television is examined
abstract: Two of the most dynamic television technologies are cable television and direct-broadcast satellites. Both are being actively pursued in both the United States and abroad. Cable television is the older of the two technologies and is well established in the United States; one of its most active promises is its capability of carrying not only television images but also data and voice communications. Broadcasting television programming to individual homes directly from a satellite in orbit around the earth is perhaps the most ambitious of all the technologies, with its promise of bringing television programming to many viewers who now receive fewer than two or three channels (or perhaps even no television at all). However, the technology is still sufficiently new that there are many unanswered questions about its technical and economic feasibility over the next few years.

articleTitle: Low-temperature reactors for space heating: Simply constructed nuclear plants are being used in the USSR to provide heat at a cost substantially below that of oil-fired plants
abstract: Nuclear generation of electric power is on the defensive in most of the world today. Manufacturers and operators of nuclear power plants are encountering not only increasing public concern over safety, but also increasing costs and a slowdown in the growth of electricity demand. These factors have crippled the nuclear power industry in the United States and hampered it elsewhere. However, engineers in the Soviet Union, Canada, Sweden, and France are developing a new use for nuclear energy that they hope will help counter the negative trends. The new application is in space heating.
