articleTitle: The message was electric: Images of electricity were first exploited to sell Victorian products; such advertising helped give electricity itself a high profile and promote technological progress
abstract: Nobody sells electricity anymore. So taken for granted is it in our lives that it goes unmentioned and uncredited when electrical appliance manufacturers tout their wares. Even power companies now“ “sell” efficiency and goodwill - it is no longer considered appropriate to encourage the public to purchase electric power. Yet it has not always been this way. Indeed, electricity has been one of the most exciting and telling themes in American advertising.

articleTitle: The way it was: A renowned educator gives a firsthand account of the decades that shaped EE education
abstract: Electrical engineering has been noted for its revolutions - major advances that open new vistas of technical opportunity. Today we expect electrical engineering education to follow these changes, but educational change has often been slow, especially as the revolutions have come more rapidly in recent years.

articleTitle: Thomas A. Edison: Flamboyant inventor: Shrewd and nonconformist in many respects, Edison helped create modern electrical engineering, yet he never became a professional engineer himself
abstract: In the spring of 1884 Thomas A. Edison was one of the small group of prominent men interested in electrical technology who issued an invitation from New York City for others to join them in founding the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. But while Edison lent his name to the formation of the first U.S. society of electrical engineers and even served nominally as one of its directors during its first year, he did not play any active role in the professional life of the group.

articleTitle: Riding the biggest wave: Entrepreneur Andrew Kay is betting that his brand of humanistic management will ensure Kaypro's survival in the turbulent PC waters
abstract: During the summer of 1962, psychologist Abraham Maslow was “a son of Visiting Fellow” at a small Del Mar., Calif., manufacturer of digital instruments then called Non-Linear Systems Inc. (NLS) and in 1983 renamed the Kaypro Corp. Maslow, who is known for his psychological “hierarchy of needs,” and Kaypro's feisty founder and president, Andrew F. Kay, talked often about the principles of “humanistic management” that Kay practiced and that Maslow pondered in a journal later published as Eupsychian Management. Kay remembers Maslow's parting words were that he believed those humanistic management principles would hold when a company was prospering but he wasn't so sure they would work “in stormy weather.”

articleTitle: The education marketplace: Instructional television: Last year 70 000 engineers enrolled in 2000 courses delivered by video technology; over 3000 Master of Science degrees were earned via TV in the last two decades
abstract: Engineers at the Hewlett-Packard Co. plant in Palo Alto, Calif., who want to stay on top of their fields are going to school - and they are doing is without leaving the HP plant. The school, Stanford University in Palo Alto, comes to them via television.

articleTitle: Turning neutrons into electricity: Spurred on by recent scientific triumphs at Princeton and Culham, England, engineers take up the challenge of designing practical fusion reactors that can compete with fossil-fuel power plants
abstract: At a demonstration power plant in Chicago in the year 2010, a fusion reactor engineered for commercial power production delivers 1200 megawatts of electricity to the local grid. Called Starfire, it is generating electricity at a cost comparable to that of neighboring oil- and coal-fired power plants. Government studies predict a worldwide depletion of oil resources by the middle of the century, and a potential cutoff of Middle East oil supplies is imminent because of political hostilities. Meanwhile, environmental groups have gained the favor of politicians in the mid-western and eastern states, amid rising reports of worsening air pollution and atmospheric carbon dioxide buildup linked in part to coal-fired plants. The fusion reactor constitutes the first implementation of the nation's long-term energy option.

articleTitle: The current issues: Formal education: EE programs
abstract: Since breaking away from physics departments in the late 1800s, electrical engineering programs have been characterized by change. Beginning with curricula based largely on electric-power concepts, the programs underwent their first major overhaul in the 1940s, when Government funding of research led to an emphasis on analog electronics. Today EE education is in the midst of another upheaval as it reflects the boom in digital electronics.

articleTitle: Nurturing energy infants and orphans: One full-time director is responsible for the DOE's Division of Advanced Energy Projects, overseeing its $10 million budget and caring for projects that no one else wants
abstract: Steven Jones of the Idaho National Engineering Laboratory has an idea that might possibly produce a thermonuclear fusion reactor that operates not at temperatures of hundreds of millions of degrees, but at room temperature. He is using nuclear particles called muons to catalyze fusion reactions - and has achieved modest successes.

articleTitle: NRC as referee: Voluminous studies of TMI have helped the Nuclear Regulatory Commission generate an action plan to alter existing nuclear reactors
abstract: Few areas of the U.S. nuclear power business remain untouched by the accident at Three Mile Island Unit 2. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission has also undergone change because of recommendations flowing from the investigations of that emergency. All the reviews and investigations set out to find some magic formula to explain “why TMI-2 went wrong.” But the studies underscored what was already known: that nuclear power operation is highly complex, and no substitute exists for a painstakingly rigorous approach to every aspect of power-plant design, construction, and operation.

articleTitle: Overcoming formidable hurdles: Engineers who are disabled, female, nondegreed, foreign-born, or retrained and a disadvantaged student reveal how to succeed despite difficulties
abstract: Finding the time and energy to pursue continuing education after long work hours, tough assignments, and deadline pressures is hard enough. The effort is even greater for engineers who have additional hurdles to overcome - those who are physically handicapped, female, or have no college degree. Others come from another country, or have been retrained into a new field. Financially disadvantaged students from another culture also face added challenges.

articleTitle: Learning from elsewhere: Incidents at sites other than TMI have expanded the nuclear knowledge base and may help contribute to the solutions of new and old problems
abstract: Even if the 1979 Three Mile Island reactor accident had not occurred, the 1980s would probably still be a traumatic period for the nuclear power industry. After a surge of growth in the 1960s and 1970s, prompted by forecasts of swelling demand for electricity, the industry has been slowed - some would say stalled - by an unexpected downturn in consumer needs and a welter of problems in operating and building reactors.

articleTitle: The case for giant particle accelerators: Particle collisions can yield a better understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and energy
abstract: Physicists hope to use a new generation of larger and more powerful particle accelerators to test existing theories of the ultimate structure of matter. The huge machines, some of which will be 50 kilometers in diameter, will accelerate particles, such as electrons and protons, to extremely high energies and cause them to collide. From the results of these collisions, it is hoped, may come clues not only to the makeup of matter but also to the nature of the forces that bind particles together and even those forces that underlie the generation of all energy in the universe.

articleTitle: An electric centura: Variations on a theme by Oppenheimer: Looking both ways from 1984, this celebration of the IEEE's Centennial addresses the give-and-take between electrotechnology and civilization
abstract: Tema - Dvorak's E-Miaor, From the New World, by a master from the Old. This theme is basic to the Variazinol

articleTitle: Buying, selling, and trading technology: What technologies can engineers export? What information can they exchange? Here's an update on U.S. technology-transfer controls
abstract: Exhibit 1: a computer chip stamped in Cyrillic letters by its Soviet manufacturer. Stephen Bryen tossed it on the desk in his office at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C. "That chip was designed in the U.S.," he said. "Now the Soviets have it."

articleTitle: A communications network for the Summer Olympics: Behind-the-scenes communicating at the Games in Los Angeles seemed a complicated and thankless task, yet AT&T took it on
abstract: The challenge was to create an easily operated communications network for the 50 000 administrators, athletes, coaches, trainers, members of support staffs, and journalists who will be in the Los Angeles basin for the Games of the XXIII Olympiad this month. The network would allow all of these individuals to communicate with each other from the many sites of the Los Angeles Games. Each of the groups, however, required a different set of functions to support its job at the Olympic Games. The only requirement common to all turned out to be a further challenge: people must be able to learn how to operate the terminal for the network in minutes - with little or no instruction. The network would have to cover an area of 4500 square miles and leave no trace when disassembled after the Olympics. Because most of the support functions at the Olympic Games would be dependent on its operation, it would have to be highly reliable.

articleTitle: Alaska plans a big switch: Most of its electricity is oil-generated, but the construction of new hydroelectric stations is expected to increase electrification throughout the state
abstract: One of the largest reservoirs of hydroelectric power in the United States " nearly 170 gigawatts " remains largely unexploited. This power, almost half of the country's potential, is available in Alaska. Yet 88 percent of the electricity actually generated in the state comes from the burning of fossil fuels. The state government is implementing an ambitious plan to change that. The plan will use some of Alaska's enormous, present-day oil income to build hydroelectric power plants, which, it is hoped, will shield Alaskan residents from electric-rate increases for decades.

articleTitle: A slow comeback: The optimists have been disappointed in the rate of progress in cleanup, but the outlook for its defueling may be brightening
abstract: “We've made so little progress in the cleanup in five years that it is literally a national disgrace,” Harold Denton, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission's director of nuclear reactor regulation, told Spectrum. Such a strong statement from the head of the office charged with regulating the industry - and therefore the cleanup of the damaged Unit 2 reactor at Three Mile Island in Middletown, Pa. - may not be surprising. But even Herman Dieckamp, the president and chief operating officer of General Public Utilities Corp. of Parsippany, N.J., which owns the facility, conceded that “in 1979, I probably thought that the bulk of the job would be done in five years.”

articleTitle: Engineering workstations: A field report: Interviews with engineers having access to CAE workstations yield mixed responses; amidst the praise are complaints of insufficient power and excess complexity
abstract: Engineers who use computer-aided engineering workstations for electronic design say the equipment significantly increases their productivity and enables them to handle more complex jobs on tighter schedules than is possible with manual methods. On the other hand, the same engineers complain that workstations are slow to execute commands, sometimes cumbersome to use, and generally difficult to integrate into the overall production cycle. Interviews with engineers at five companies using CAE workstations revealed that although some perceptions of workstation capabilities are common to almost all installations, opinions about their overall usefulness vary depending on the kind of work the companies do, their particular engineering environments, and the ratio of engineers to workstations.

articleTitle: William D. Coolidge: Shirt-sleeves manager: Famous for two wide-ranging inventions, this engineer proved himself an innovative manager as he guided the renowned GE Research Laboratory through some of its most turbulent years
abstract: 33Coolidge arrived to commence work.“Thus did the founder of General Electric Co.'s Research Laboratory, Willis R. Whitney, record the arrival of his famous successor on Sept. 11, 1905. Whitney's laconic notebook entry gives little inkling that he recognized how truly fortunate GE was to have snared William D. Coolidge. Whitney's second-in-command at the time, Laurence A. Hawkins, would later describe Coolidge as Whitney's“most resourceful experimenter and right-hand man.”

articleTitle: Continuing education: A view from the top: How to apply a formal education and continue the learning process is one of the issues nine successful engineers discuss
abstract: In every successful career, a magic threshold is crossed. One can see, with stunning clarity, how everything in education, in professional and personal experiences, and even in personal failures, contributed to that success.

articleTitle: Band-aids and better: Hardware, instrumentation, and operations are improving on a piecemeal basis and more systematic studies are under way
abstract: Before the Three Mile island accident in 1979, safety measures built into nuclear reactors and control rooms focused on improbable catastrophic accident scenarios and the weaknesses of the machine. Only minor attention was paid to the role of plant operators and emergency procedures. Now the focus is on lesser, more probable events and on the man-machine interface.

articleTitle: But challenges remain: The issues may be clearer and the problems better defined, but solutions may not be simple and will often involve negotiation and compromise
abstract: With all the attention focused on nuclear power ills, the fact remains that 1 3 percent of the electricity used in the United States today is generated by nuclear power plants. They will continue to be run, but they must be operated safely and efficiently. And with all the recent press coverage of plant cancellations, it is easily forgotten that 42 more plants are still under construction. If they are to be completed even nearly on time and reasonably within budget, they must be completed efficiently, and if they are to operate safely, quality construction must be ensured.

articleTitle: A framework for the future: Industry joins Government in establishing campus beachheads, as technology begins to transform university life
abstract: It is a university that has only administrative offices at its sole campus in Fort Collins, Colo, Its faculty members reside in nine states, its students are scattered throughout the United States, and degree offerings are only at the Master of Science level [p. 108]. The National Technological University is the first to offer these degrees solely through video technology. A supporting consortium of 24 schools prepares and video-tapes the courses, which are then distributed by NTU to industrial and government clients who provide classroom sites. In Ihe offing are satellite-enhanced communications.

articleTitle: The great culture machine: brainwasher or educator?
abstract: Some would argue that electrotechnology in the form of films, radio, and television has done more to educate humanity than all the efforts of our schools—but is that good or bad? Television today is the central cultural arm of American society. From infancy on, children learn more about society from TV than from school, their parents, or any other source. TV's role is like that of religion in preindustrial society—TV is today's religion.

articleTitle: Taming the world's greatest tokamak: Diverse electrotechnical disciplines are used to probe, test, measure, and analyze a premier fusion reactor
abstract: At Princeton University's Plasma Physics Laboratory, scores of electrical and electronics engineers are applying diverse disciplines to the job at hand: advancing fusion engineering to the point where commercial electric power based on fusion reactions may one day become feasible. At the laboratory, these engineers must continually meet the challenge of designing systems to probe, test, measure, and analyze the world's most advanced operating reactor of its type. The challenge entails mastering, as well as merging, tools and techniques from fields spanning power engineering, magnetics, instrumentation, data acquisition, data processing, computers, and computer graphics.

articleTitle: Power and energy: Slowed electricity demand and high interest rates have forced utilities to generate, transmit, and distribute power more efficiently
abstract: Because of the continued slow growth in electricity demand and the high cost of fossil fuels, utilities in the United States placed a high priority on saving money last year and improving the efficiency of generation, transmission, and distribution components. More emphasis was placed on high-voltage dc for efficient transmission of electricity over long distances and for linking back-to-back ac networks. Amorphous metals were used in the cores of new distribution and power transformers to decrease the energy wasted through core losses. And advances in superconducting generators also were aimed at saving energy.

articleTitle: The engineer's job: It moves toward abstraction: Automated modeling and analysis minimize the practitioner's contact with real hardware
abstract: As engineering tasks have become more complex and the tools available to grapple with them have become increasingly sophisticated, the job of electrical engineering has become more analytical and abstract. Far more emphasis is being placed on designing a product that will work properly the first time it is built, rather than on making a series of prototypes and debugging them. This trend toward analysis and modeling is changing the way engineers work, both individually and as members of organizations.
